title: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026
content:
Event detail Information Date Tuesday, 29 September 2026 Main conference JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi My role Attendee at the Ho Chi Minh City watch party Event overview AWS brought together engineers, customers and community builders for more than 30 sessions, alongside an expo, startup showcases and a community area. The Hanoi program opened at 07:30, with a 09:00 keynote, technical sessions from 11:00 and a 17:00 close. The keynote lineup included Amazon CTO Werner Vogels, Katalon’s Mai Le and Techcombank CEO Jens Lottner. The agenda also identified a Ho Chi Minh City watch-party session and listed talks on topics such as VPBank’s internal developer platform on EKS and taking agentic AI from a demo to deployment.
At the Ho Chi Minh City watch party with fellow attendees. What I learned Follow an incident across services In a demo I photographed, GoTymeX investigated a login outage that first showed up as a spike in HTTP 5xx errors at the gateway. The team checked metrics, logs, traces, and recent changes, then followed requests through the downstream services. They found a query waiting on a metadata lock on an Aurora MySQL reader. That explained why requests were piling up and why a service further up the chain was timing out.
I noticed that AWS DevOps Agent had read-only access for the investigation. An engineer still had to approve a change like stopping a query. GoTymeX looked at six months of incidents and reported that the median time from an alert to the first likely cause fell from 34.5 to 10 minutes. That tells me how quickly the team had something to investigate.
The GoTyme demonstration connected gateway errors to a database lock several services downstream. Verify the identity a workload actually uses Kha Van’s conference recap described pairing a Kubernetes service account with an IAM role using Amazon EKS Pod Identity. The application can obtain temporary AWS credentials through the SDK. An environment variable or another credential source earlier in the SDK’s chain can change which identity the application uses. If a permission error occurs, checking the caller identity inside the workload helps distinguish a missing permission from a workload using the wrong role.
Design for the work that follows the demo Kha Van’s recap described how internal developer platforms let teams repeat the same deployment steps. It also raised a question about AI agents in production. Who owns the agent, what can it do, and where can the team see what it did? The infrastructure examples solved different problems. Direct Connect in Hanoi gives organizations a private path to AWS, and Hanoi Local Zone can put resources closer to users. The choice depends on the latency users see, where the data has to live, and what the team can operate.
How this relates to Ownword I’d use the same approach if Ownword users couldn’t sign in or save a word. I’d log the step that failed, the time, and the component that returned the error. That would give the team enough to trace whether the problem started at sign-in, in the API, or in storage without recording credentials or user content.

What I learned Define a task that can be evaluated The judging criteria made me think about what a team could show in a short demo. I’d start with an agent that answers a common support question using a small set of documents. Show a question with a known answer and the passage that supports it. Then try a question the documents don’t cover so the reviewer can see how the agent handles it.
Give prompts, retrieval and tools distinct jobs The practical block covered prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), knowledge bases and agents. The prompt defines the task and response format. A knowledge base gives the model a collection to retrieve relevant material from. An agent can choose a permitted tool to take a further step. Test what happens when the evidence is weak When I test an agent, I’d check whether the source it cites actually supports the answer and what happens when the source is missing or stale. I’d ask one clear question, one that needs clarification, and one the knowledge base can’t answer. If the agent can edit records, I’d also check that asking it to read something leaves the records as they were.
Explain design decisions in terms of the user The career talk and Q&A gave me a way to present a project in an interview or demo. I’d describe a problem the user has and explain one decision I made. Then I’d show a result or a test the audience could reproduce.

title: Proposal
content:
Executive summary Ownword is an English learning app for people who recognize more words than they can use when they write. It gives learners a way to find the word they’re reaching for, save it, and practice until they can recall it on their own. A separate Writing module helps them decide what to change in a draft and check how well a revision addresses that feedback.
The pilot runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock handles concept search with Kimi K3.1 Pro, and OpenRouter gives the Writing module access to a frontier model for draft assessment and revision feedback. Readers can watch the demo video, try the live app, or deploy their own copy with the bilingual workshop.
At report close (30 November 2026), we are still waiting for AWS Support to resolve model access. Requests for GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock returned AccessDeniedException on our AWS Free Tier account even after we accepted the model agreement. We continue to access GPT-6 Luna through OpenRouter for evaluation. After several rounds of benchmarking for draft assessment and revision checks, we selected GPT-6.1 Terra with low reasoning effort through OpenRouter for production Writing because it offered the best balance of feedback quality and cost for our workload. For vocabulary enrichment and practice grading, we picked Gemini 3.6 Flash through OpenRouter because it gave reliable definitions and grading at low cost, and Gemini 3.6 Flash is not listed in the Amazon Bedrock model catalog.
The problem You can recognize a word in a book and still reach for a simpler one when you write. Looking up a better word helps you finish the sentence. The next time you need that word, you may have to look it up again. Revising can be just as frustrating when a sentence feels off and you can’t pinpoint what to change.
Ownword starts from a learner’s own draft or an idea they want to express. It connects that moment of discovery to later practice and keeps writing feedback tied to the passages the learner wrote.
Audience and learning loop The pilot is designed for advanced English learners working on their own. The vocabulary loop moves through six steps: write, discover, choose, practice, retrieve, and activate. On WordBoard, a saved word progresses through New, Practicing, and Active as the learner recalls and uses it in different contexts over time.
Imagine wanting a word for an experience that feels happy and sad at the same time. You can describe that feeling in English or Vietnamese, consider a suggestion like bittersweet, and save it to WordBoard. In Quick Review you can flag the word if you forget it. In Full Practice you can try recalling it and using it in a sentence on a topic of your choice.
Writing follows a separate loop. The learner picks a prompt, writes a response, reads feedback on specific passages, and revises in their own words. Keeping the original in view lets the learner see what changed and check which earlier suggestions the revision addresses.
Pilot scope Feature What the pilot supports Vocabulary discovery Find suggestions in your own writing or describe a concept in English or Vietnamese. Save useful suggestions or add a word by hand. WordBoard and practice Track saved words, listen to browser-based pronunciation, review words you forgot, and practice recall and sentence use. The learning streak tracks days of activity. Writing Draft from a prompt, review feedback on exact passages, and revisit the original and its revision in Writing history. Accounts Sign in with email and password or Google. An eligible existing account can link to a verified Google identity and keep its WordBoard. The pilot uses one application VM and a private Single-AZ database. Its purpose is to test the complete learning and recovery flows with a small group.
Deployed architecture Ownword production architecture and automated releases, 24 November 2026. Select the diagram to open it at full size. AWS services used Amazon CloudFront. Serves the public HTTPS entry point for Ownword and forwards web and API requests to the Caddy origin on Lightsail. Cognito callbacks use the public app hostname. AWS WAF. Applies a web ACL to requests that reach the CloudFront distribution. It operates at the public edge before those requests go to the origin. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Supplies the viewer certificate for the public hostname on CloudFront. Caddy handles the certificate for the separate origin connection. Amazon Lightsail. Runs the Singapore VM. Caddy accepts origin HTTPS and forwards traffic to Next.js over the private Docker network. The VM also runs the database backup and backup health jobs. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Stores application records such as learner profiles, WordBoard entries, practice results, and Writing history. The encrypted Single-AZ database runs in a private subnet in Singapore (ap-southeast-1a) and accepts connections on port 5432 only from the Lightsail host over VPC peering. The app verifies the database certificate and hostname. Amazon Cognito. Manages passwords, verified email, and the Google sign-in flow through a user pool in Singapore. Next.js maps the verified Cognito identity to the learner’s PostgreSQL record. AWS Lambda. Runs the Pre sign-up trigger for Google federation in Singapore. When the first Google sign-in matches an eligible existing account, the trigger can link the verified identity so the learner keeps their WordBoard. Amazon Bedrock. Runs Kimi K3.1 Pro for concept search through a U.S. inference profile. The application calls the Bedrock endpoint in N. Virginia and validates the suggestions before returning them. Amazon S3. Holds daily PostgreSQL exports in a private bucket and writes access logs to a separate private bucket. Both use SSE-S3. A copy outside the app VM and database gives the team an archive it can restore into a separate test database. Amazon ECR. Stores private release images built by GitHub Actions. Lightsail pulls the published image by digest and checks the app after rollout. Release flow Amazon CloudWatch. Receives the hourly BackupFresh metric. The backup alarm evaluates whether the latest export is fresh and its S3 copy is present. Amazon SNS. Sends an email to the operator when the CloudWatch alarm changes to the alarm state. AWS Key Management Service (KMS). Provides the customer-managed key that encrypts the SNS topic used by the backup alarm. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Scopes AWS permissions for Bedrock calls, S3 backup access, CloudWatch metric writes, and the account-linking Lambda. PostgreSQL has separate roles for the app and backup job. Technical implementation Request and data flow Open the app (steps 1-4): The browser connects to CloudFront over HTTPS. CloudFront then connects over TLS to Caddy at the origin hostname. Caddy sends the request to Next.js, which reads or writes learner data in private RDS using a separate TLS connection. Sign in (steps 5-8): A password sign-in goes to Cognito. For Google sign-in, Cognito handles federation and returns the browser to Ownword’s callback. Next.js exchanges the authorization code using PKCE. The Lambda trigger can link the Google identity during the first eligible sign-in. Ask a model (steps 9-10): Next.js sends concept-search requests to Kimi on Bedrock. Writing assessment, vocabulary enrichment, and practice grading use separate OpenRouter routes. Provider credentials stay on the server. Back up and alert (steps 11-14): The VM reads RDS with a read-only backup role, exports the database to private S3, and checks the latest backup each hour. A stale or missing signal triggers an email through the encrypted SNS topic. The workshop walks through the diagram and request flow, sign-in and public HTTPS, and backup, restore, and alarm testing.
How we use Amazon Bedrock and OpenRouter Ownword uses Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock for concept search, a core part of its vocabulary discovery. Learners can describe an idea in English or Vietnamese and get suggestions for words and phrases that express it. The app can reuse a saved result for a repeat lookup, which avoids another model call.
Writing submits the draft or revision to GPT-6.1 Terra Low through OpenRouter and requests Zero Data Retention on the configured route. Vocabulary enrichment and practice grading use Gemini 3.6 Flash through OpenRouter for reliable short responses at low cost, and Gemini is not on Bedrock. The application validates the structured feedback before saving it. Model access status
Timeline and milestones Milestone What happened 14 September to 18 October Worked through the AWS labs on accounts, IAM, networking, databases, and monitoring. Worklog 25 October Recorded the first Ownword prototype with draft-based vocabulary discovery, WordBoard, and sentence practice. Week 6 28 October Added Quick Review and Full Practice so learners could focus on words they had forgotten. Week 7 5 November Verified the backup path by restoring an S3 dump and testing the CloudWatch and SNS alert flow on the Lightsail pilot. Week 8 12 November Deployed the custom account screens, Google sign-in, and pronunciation controls. Week 9 20 November Moved the application database to private RDS and released the daily learning streak. 30 November Rehearsed the demo, captured the Workshop test results, and finished the handover. Cost estimate and optimization For a 10-learner pilot, the operating budget is US$43.56/month before tax and account credits. This combines US$43.24 for AWS and US$0.32 for OpenRouter inference at published rates. At 100 learners with the same server sizes, the estimate rises to US$60.98/month.
Monthly cost 10 active learners 100 active learners Lightsail and private RDS $33.01 $33.01 Edge, security, storage and monitoring $8.69 $9.33 Bedrock concept search $1.54 $15.40 OpenRouter Writing, vocabulary and practice $0.32 $3.24 Total $43.56 $60.98 The detailed Workshop estimate records the AWS Pricing Calculator inputs and results, request and token assumptions, and applicable allowances. We control costs by reusing concept-search results, setting provider spend limits, and limiting backup and release-image retention.
Design choices and risks Risk What the design does and what to check The app VM goes down RDS keeps the database separate from the app host. Use the workshop to rehearse redeployment and time how long it takes for sign-in and WordBoard to return. Database failure or stale backup The pilot uses Single-AZ RDS. Keep a private S3 copy of each daily dump and check BackupFresh. Time a restore into an isolated database and record which backup it used. Access to another learner’s data Cognito establishes identity. Next.js limits access to the signed-in owner’s records. Check that a second account cannot open a saved-word detail URL from the first account. Model failure or unsuitable feedback Validate response structure before using it. Test a fresh concept lookup and a revision with synthetic text so a provider error or unhelpful result is visible. Higher usage or costs Use the saved result for repeat lookups and cap model calls. Compare CPU, memory, latency, and errors under a small test load before deciding whether the VM needs more capacity. Delivery and measurement The report includes the architecture diagram, the live app, and a bilingual deployment and cleanup guide. Earlier release checks recorded Cognito sign-in, persistence of saved words and practice results, live model calls, and a restore of an RDS backup into a temporary database.
The demo is successful if a learner can find an unfamiliar word, save and recall it later, and work through feedback on a draft. The AWS side is successful if the team can repeat the lab with its own resources, restore the data, and receive an alert when the backup is stale. The Workshop verification chapter records a valid request and its saved database row, a CloudWatch log from the sign-in flow, and the response to invalid input. Workshop acceptance checks

title: EC2, Lightsail, or Lambda? Which Is Right for a Small Project?
content:
Publication detail Information Publication date 16 November 2026 Publication link Original Vietnamese post on Facebook Publication topic Choosing between Amazon EC2, Amazon Lightsail, and AWS Lambda for small projects A portfolio site and a job that sends order confirmations have different needs. I use examples like these to compare the three services. EC2 gives you more control over the server and network, and you handle updates, security, and monitoring. Lightsail has a bundle that’s easier to set up for a portfolio or a small storefront. Lambda can send a confirmation when an order comes in.
As traffic grows, you can put a load balancer in front of EC2 and add Auto Scaling. Lambda has a limit on how long each call can run. If you use it to serve an API, include anything else you’ll need, such as API Gateway or a database, when you work out the cost. I’d also factor in how much time you want to spend running it.

title: Architecture and data flow
content:
Production request flow Ownword production architecture and automated releases. Select the diagram to open it at full size. Steps Follow the path 1-3. Public HTTPS and origin The browser connects to app.ownword.co through CloudFront, with an ACM viewer certificate and an AWS WAF web ACL. CloudFront connects over TLS to Caddy at origin.ownword.co. Caddy forwards requests to Next.js on port 3000 inside the private Docker Compose network. 4. Database Next.js reads and writes to private Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in Singapore over Lightsail VPC peering. The Single-AZ database runs in a private subnet in ap-southeast-1a, encrypts storage with the AWS-managed RDS key, and accepts TLS connections on port 5432 only from the Lightsail host’s private address. 5-8. Sign-in Next.js talks to Amazon Cognito in Singapore for password sign-in and OAuth code exchange. The browser follows Cognito’s OAuth flow for Google sign-in and returns through /auth/callback, where Next.js exchanges the code using PKCE. On the first eligible federated sign-in, Cognito can invoke its Pre sign-up Lambda in Singapore to link the verified Google identity. Next.js resolves the Cognito identity to the learner record in PostgreSQL. 9-10. Model requests Concept search calls Amazon Bedrock through the N. Virginia endpoint using the Kimi K3.1 Pro U.S. inference profile. Writing assessment calls GPT-6.1 Terra Low through OpenRouter, and vocabulary enrichment and practice grading call Gemini 3.6 Flash through OpenRouter (Gemini models are not on Bedrock). All model calls originate on the server. 11-14. Backup and alert The Lightsail backup job reads RDS under a separate database role, makes a daily PostgreSQL dump, and uploads it to a private S3 backup bucket. Backups and the separate access-log bucket use SSE-S3. An hourly check publishes BackupFresh. A stale or missing signal triggers CloudWatch to notify the operator through an SNS topic encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Release flow A push to release/lightsail starts GitHub Actions. The workflow checks the code, builds a Docker image, and uses short-lived AWS credentials through GitHub OIDC to publish it to private Amazon ECR in Singapore. Lightsail checks ECR every two minutes. On a new image, it pulls the exact digest, runs migrations against RDS, and checks the home and sign-in routes after restarting the app. If startup fails, it restores the previous app image.
AWS Well-Architected pillar alignment Pillar How Ownword applies it Operational excellence GitHub Actions checks TypeScript and tests before building immutable ECR images, and Lightsail pulls releases by digest with automatic rollback on failed health checks. Hourly BackupFresh metrics and a CloudWatch alarm surface backup issues early. Security CloudFront and AWS WAF sit in front of the origin. RDS runs in a private subnet with encryption at rest, security-group ingress restricted to the Lightsail private /32, and verify-full TLS. Cognito uses PKCE for OAuth, model keys stay on the server, and IAM policies separate Bedrock, S3 backup, and account-linking permissions. Reliability Moving PostgreSQL off the Lightsail host into RDS separates application and database failures. Daily pg_dump archives are copied to versioned private S3 with SHA-256 verification and tested via isolated container restores, while the backup alarm treats missing data as breaching. The Single-AZ database is a deliberate pilot tradeoff documented with its recovery path. Performance efficiency CloudFront terminates viewer HTTPS at edge locations and forwards requests to Singapore (ap-southeast-1) close to target learners. RDS runs on ARM-based db.t4g.micro (Graviton) with gp3 storage, and the app reuses saved Bedrock concept-search results on repeat lookups to avoid unnecessary model latency. Cost optimization Fixed hosting stays predictable on a 2 GB Lightsail bundle and Single-AZ db.t4g.micro. Repeat concept-search caching, output-token limits, OpenRouter spend caps, S3 lifecycle expiration (30 days current, 7 days noncurrent), and ECR image retention keep variable costs bounded. See chapter 5.7. Deployment used in the lab Start by setting up Lightsail and private RDS with your own lab resources. You’ll use two DNS names. Cognito sends users back to the public hostname after sign-in, and Caddy serves the origin hostname. A separate PostgreSQL role reads the data for backups. Later, you’ll try a restore in an isolated PostgreSQL container.
Checkpoint. Follow a user request to RDS, a stale-backup alert to the operator’s inbox, and a release image from GitHub to Lightsail.

title: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels
content:
Event detail Information Event theme Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam Date Friday, 2 October 2026 Location Ho Chi Minh City Guest Dr. Werner Vogels, Chief Technology Officer at Amazon My role Attendee Event overview At the First Cloud AI Journey fireside chat, Dr. Vogels talked about database outages at Amazon, keeping services available, and paying for cloud resources as you use them. He also discussed what engineers are responsible for when they use AI. What stuck with me was how often he started with a problem that users or operators had before getting into the technology.
The opening slide for the 2 October fireside chat. What I learned Start with the way the application reads and writes data After a peak shopping-season outage, Amazon examined what its applications were asking the database to do. A large share of requests were key lookups, such as finding a shopping cart by its ID. That observation helped motivate Dynamo, Amazon’s distributed key-value system and an influence on DynamoDB. Dynamo’s design prioritized availability for those operations and used object versions to help resolve conflicting writes when needed. My takeaway was to list the common reads and writes before choosing a database, then decide how the application should behave when a read is stale or a write is retried.
Measure the slow requests and rehearse recovery The discussion on operational excellence gave me two ways to check that an application behaves as intended. The first is to look at tail latency. If P99.9 is two seconds, roughly 99.9% of observed requests completed within two seconds, while the slowest fraction took longer. A median can look healthy while those users are still waiting. The second is to run a GameDay, a planned exercise that introduces a failure and checks that detection, failover and recovery work together. A useful exercise records when an alert fired, who acted on it and which user operations recovered.
Budget for the reliability a workload needs Vogels also talked about how paying for cloud resources by usage changes what teams invest in. I’d ask what a proposed change actually buys us. Extra capacity or redundancy can be worth it if it protects a user workflow we care about. For a small pilot, I’d start by working out the monthly cost and trying the recovery steps.
Dr. Werner Vogels in conversation during the fireside chat. Keep ownership when using AI Vogels’s “Renaissance developer” combines technical depth with curiosity, systems thinking and clear communication. I understood this as knowing enough about the neighboring parts of a system to see where a change might cause trouble. If AI helps draft a change to a sign-in flow, the engineer still has to understand the session behavior, review the permissions and test both successful and failed attempts.
How this relates to Ownword A slow sign-in, word lookup, or WordBoard reload is easy to notice in Ownword. I’d time each one so a good overall average can’t hide a single slow step. For a recovery exercise, I’d test whether a failed lookup gives a clear message, lets me retry, and leaves the words I’d already saved accessible.

title: What Happens When Your Website Suddenly Gets 10,000 Visitors?
content:
Publication detail Information Publication date 17 November 2026 Publication link Original Vietnamese post on Facebook Publication topic Handling a website traffic spike with Application Load Balancer, EC2 Auto Scaling, and CloudWatch Picture a small online shop during an 11/11 sale. When a lot of shoppers arrive at once, pages may take longer to load and some requests may fail. How much the site slows down depends on how many people are active at the same time and what each request asks the server to do, such as signing someone in or querying the database.
An Application Load Balancer uses health checks to send requests to healthy targets. EC2 Auto Scaling adjusts the number of instances using signals like CPU utilization or requests per target. CloudWatch shows how busy or slow the site is and can send an alert when a metric crosses its threshold. New instances take time to start, and adding them won’t necessarily speed up a database that’s already overloaded.

title: Prepare Lightsail and private RDS
content:
1. Create the Lightsail host and origin DNS In Lightsail → Instances → Create instance, choose Singapore, Linux/Unix → OS Only → Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, and an x86-64 bundle with a public IPv4 address and at least 2 GB RAM. Name it ownword-lab. Save the private IPv4 from the instance page. Select an SSH key you already hold or download the matching private key from the Lightsail account’s SSH keys page. Create a static IPv4 in Singapore and attach it to the instance. In your DNS provider, point your origin subdomain, for example origin-lab.example.com, directly to that address with an A record (DNS-only if your provider offers a proxy). If you do not own a domain, skip the DNS record and use origin-lab.<A-B-C-D>.sslip.io (your static IPv4 with hyphens instead of dots) as the origin hostname; sslip.io resolves it to your instance automatically so Caddy can issue a public TLS certificate. The public app hostname is configured with CloudFront in chapter 5.5. In the Lightsail networking firewall, allow TCP 80 and 443 for Caddy’s public certificate validation and HTTPS. Restrict TCP 22 to your workstation’s public IP. If you use Lightsail browser SSH, enable its separate access option. Leave ports 3000 and 5432 closed on the internet. Review IPv6 rules separately if enabled. Lightsail instance creation · Static IP · Lightsail firewall Checkpoint. The instance is running, your origin hostname resolves to the static IPv4, and you can connect as ubuntu.
2. Create a private PostgreSQL instance In Lightsail → Account → Advanced, enable VPC peering for Singapore. The receiving VPC must be the account’s default VPC in Singapore. In the VPC console, confirm that the peering connection is active and the route tables for the RDS subnets have a route to the Lightsail network through that peering connection. Use the actual routes and CIDRs shown in your account. In that default VPC, use a DB subnet group covering at least two Availability Zones. Create a dedicated security group for the DB with inbound TCP 5432 from the Lightsail instance’s private IPv4 /32. Attach that group to RDS and remove any broader ingress that the creation wizard added. In RDS → Databases → Create database → Standard create, select PostgreSQL 16, a Single DB instance, db.t4g.micro if available, and 20 GiB encrypted gp3. Select the default VPC, DB subnet group and security group from steps 1-2. Set Public access: No, port 5432, at least one day of automated backup retention, and deletion protection. Use a lab administrator password stored privately. Leave the initial database name blank so you can create it with the correct owner below. Lightsail VPC peering · RDS VPC and subnet groups · Create an RDS DB instance Checkpoint. RDS is Available, reports Publicly accessible: No, and gives you its DNS endpoint. Use that endpoint for TLS hostname verification.
3. Transfer the source and bootstrap Ubuntu On your workstation. Open a shell where you saved the archive and fill in the SSH key path and IP for your instance.
KEY="$HOME/.ssh/ownword-lab.pem" LIGHTSAIL_IP='YOUR_LIGHTSAIL_STATIC_IPV4' scp -i "$KEY" ownword-lab-source-c8a903e.tar.gz "ubuntu@$LIGHTSAIL_IP:~/" ssh -i "$KEY" "ubuntu@$LIGHTSAIL_IP" In the Lightsail SSH session. Unpack the archive into a new directory and run the setup script. Disconnect and sign back in so your user picks up its Docker group membership.
mkdir "$HOME/ownword-lab" tar -xzf "$HOME/ownword-lab-source-c8a903e.tar.gz" -C "$HOME/ownword-lab" cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" bash deploy/lightsail/bootstrap-ubuntu.sh After reconnecting:
cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" docker compose version free -h docker pull postgres:16-alpine install -d -m 700 deploy/lightsail/.secrets curl -fsSL https://truststore.pki.rds.amazonaws.com/global/global-bundle.pem \ -o deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-ca.pem chmod 644 deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-ca.pem The setup script installs Docker and Compose and adds 2 GiB of swap. The RDS CA bundle is public. Later, you’ll also store private environment files in .secrets. Docker on Ubuntu · RDS CA bundles
4. Create the application and backup logins In the Lightsail SSH session. Fill in your RDS endpoint and administrator name. Enter the administrator password when the container prompts you. With verify-full, PostgreSQL checks the certificate chain and matches the certificate to the endpoint hostname.
cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" RDS_HOST='YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT' RDS_ADMIN='YOUR_RDS_MASTER_USERNAME' docker run --rm -it \ --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-ca.pem,target=/rds-ca.pem,readonly" \ -e PGSSLMODE=verify-full -e PGSSLROOTCERT=/rds-ca.pem \ postgres:16-alpine psql -h "$RDS_HOST" -p 5432 -U "$RDS_ADMIN" -d postgres -W Inside psql. Run the statements once on the new instance. Generate two different random passwords, for example with openssl rand -hex 32, and enter them when prompted. The application login will own the database and run the Drizzle migrations. In chapter 5.6, you’ll grant the backup login read access once the schema exists.
\set ON_ERROR_STOP on \conninfo CREATE ROLE ownword_app LOGIN; \password ownword_app CREATE ROLE ownword_backup LOGIN; \password ownword_backup GRANT ownword_app TO CURRENT_USER WITH SET TRUE; CREATE DATABASE ownword OWNER ownword_app; \q Checkpoint. Check that \conninfo reports SSL and that both roles and the database exist. If the connection times out, check the peering connection, subnet routes, and the private IPv4 in the security group. For a certificate error, confirm you’re using the RDS endpoint and the AWS CA bundle. RDS PostgreSQL TLS · PostgreSQL database ownership
A read-only check from the running Ownword app on Lightsail confirmed a TLS 1.3 connection to production Amazon RDS in Singapore.

title: Configure sign-in, deploy Ownword and connect CloudFront
content:
1. Create the Cognito pool and public client In Amazon Cognito, Asia Pacific (Singapore), create a lab user pool with email sign-in, password authentication, self-registration, and email verification. Require only the email attribute so the Ownword form can register users. Create a public app client without a secret, such as the Single-page application client type. Use verified email for account recovery. Enable the Cognito user pool identity provider, Authorization code grant, and scopes openid email profile in the app client’s login settings. Set the callback to https://app-lab.example.com/auth/callback and sign-out URL to https://app-lab.example.com/, using your public lab hostname. Create a Cognito prefix domain and assign a managed-login branding style if required. In Authentication flows, enable username-and-password sign-in (ALLOW_USER_PASSWORD_AUTH). Ownword’s server uses USER_PASSWORD_AUTH for the custom form and the OAuth code grant with PKCE for managed login. Record the pool ID, client ID and Cognito domain. Cognito app clients · Authorization and PKCE · App client API and auth flows 2. Configure Google and link verified accounts In Google Auth Platform, configure Branding and Audience for the lab OAuth project. For a Cognito prefix domain, add amazoncognito.com under authorized domains. Request the basic OpenID, email and profile scopes. Create a Web application OAuth client. If the Google project is in testing mode, add the lab Google accounts as test users. On the Google client, set Authorized JavaScript origins to https://YOUR_PREFIX.auth.ap-southeast-1.amazoncognito.com and Authorized redirect URIs to that domain plus /oauth2/idpresponse. Then add Google in the Cognito pool using the Google client ID and secret, request openid email profile, and map Google email and email_verified to the matching Cognito attributes. Enable Google alongside Cognito user pool in the app client and make the mapped attributes writable. Google federation settings · Cognito attribute mapping Download the Singapore account-linking script and upload it to your home directory in Singapore CloudShell. Run the dry run first and verify the account, pool and mappings. Run --apply only on your lab pool. Record the function and execution role that the script creates. Wait at least 70 seconds for propagation before testing a first Google sign-in. Pre sign-up trigger · Linking federated profiles POOL_ID='ap-southeast-1_YOUR_LAB_POOL_SUFFIX' python3 ~/google-linker-cloudshell.py --pool-id "$POOL_ID" python3 ~/google-linker-cloudshell.py --pool-id "$POOL_ID" --apply aws cognito-idp describe-user-pool --region ap-southeast-1 --user-pool-id "$POOL_ID" \ --query 'UserPool.LambdaConfig.PreSignUp' --output text If --apply stops partway through, use the suffix after the underscore in the pool ID to find any lab resources it created. The function is ownword-google-link-<suffix>, the role is ownword-google-link-role-<suffix>, and the log group is /aws/lambda/ownword-google-link-<suffix>. Check the trigger configuration before retrying. If you need a fresh attempt, detach the new trigger if it was attached, then delete the function, role and log group from that failed attempt. Keep the pool and OAuth client for the retry.
3. Prepare credentials for the model providers Check that your account can call the Kimi K3.1 Pro U.S. inference profile from N. Virginia. AWS may ask you to enable access or complete a provider subscription. Even if the profile shows Active, check that your account can invoke it. Run the commands in N. Virginia CloudShell as an administrator who can read the profile. The generated policy uses your profile ARN and the ARN of each destination model. Review both results before attaching the policy. Bedrock model access · Inference profile IAM prerequisites · GetInferenceProfile CLI aws bedrock get-inference-profile --region us-east-1 \ --inference-profile-identifier us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 > ownword-lab-profile.json jq -e '.status == "ACTIVE" and (.models | length > 0)' ownword-lab-profile.json jq '{ Version: "2012-10-17", Statement: [ {Effect:"Allow", Action:"bedrock:InvokeModel", Resource:.inferenceProfileArn}, {Effect:"Allow", Action:"bedrock:InvokeModel", Resource:[.models[].modelArn], Condition:{StringEquals:{"bedrock:InferenceProfileArn":.inferenceProfileArn}}} ] }' ownword-lab-profile.json > ownword-lab-bedrock-policy.json Attach the inline policy to a separate identity for the lab app, such as the IAM user ownword-lab-bedrock with programmatic access. Give the app its own credentials and keep them private. If you use temporary credentials, include the session token and refresh them before they expire. Keep the administrator and backup credentials separate. IAM access keys · Bedrock Converse permissions Create two lab OpenRouter keys. Use one for vocabulary and practice grading. The Writing key needs access to GPT-6.1 Terra Low with strict structured output and zero data retention. Set a spend limit at the provider. If a model call is denied, record the error and confirm access before you mark that part of the exercise complete. 4. Build and start the app against RDS This step builds the app container on Lightsail, runs the PostgreSQL migrations against RDS, and starts Caddy and Next.js.
In the Lightsail SSH session. Create both environment files from the unpacked source directory. Enter secrets in the editor. Use a different random hexadecimal password for each lab database role so the values are easy to enter in the files.
cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" umask 077 cp deploy/lightsail/.env.example deploy/lightsail/.env chmod 600 deploy/lightsail/.env nano deploy/lightsail/.env nano deploy/lightsail/.secrets/app-rds.env Set these values in deploy/lightsail/.env:
Setting Lab value APP_DOMAIN Origin hostname only, for example origin-lab.example.com APP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN Public URL, for example https://app-lab.example.com COGNITO_ISSUER https://cognito-idp.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/YOUR_POOL_ID COGNITO_DOMAIN and COGNITO_CLIENT_ID Full Cognito prefix-domain URL and the public client ID from step 1 CUSTOM_AUTH_ENABLED and GOOGLE_SIGN_IN_ENABLED Both true after steps 1 and 2 POSTGRES_PASSWORD A separate random placeholder for the base Compose file’s unused local DB service. The RDS overlay supplies the actual app password. OPENROUTER_API_KEY and OPENROUTER_MODEL Lab vocabulary key and a verified compatible model. The archive defaults to google/gemini-3.6-flash. BEDROCK_CONCEPT_MODEL us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN Bedrock runtime credentials from step 3. Leave the token empty for a long-lived IAM key. WRITING_MODULE_ENABLED and WRITING_TERRA_ENABLED Both true WRITING_TERRA_OPENROUTER_API_KEY, WRITING_TRENDS_ENABLED Separate Writing key and false for trends In deploy/lightsail/.secrets/app-rds.env, enter:
OWNWORD_RDS_HOST=YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT OWNWORD_RDS_DATABASE=ownword OWNWORD_RDS_USER=ownword_app OWNWORD_RDS_PASSWORD=YOUR_APP_ROLE_PASSWORD OWNWORD_RDS_CA_FILE=/home/ubuntu/ownword-lab/deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-ca.pem Save the helper below so the migration and app commands use the same environment files and RDS override. Source it again when you open a new SSH session, then use ownword_compose for the lab. The --no-deps flag leaves the base Compose file’s local db service off.
cat > "$HOME/ownword-lab/compose-lab.sh" <<'EOF' ownword_compose() { local app_root="$HOME/ownword-lab" docker compose --project-name ownword \ --env-file "$app_root/deploy/lightsail/.env" \ --env-file "$app_root/deploy/lightsail/.secrets/app-rds.env" \ -f "$app_root/deploy/lightsail/compose.yaml" \ -f "$app_root/deploy/lightsail/compose.rds.yaml" "$@" } EOF source "$HOME/ownword-lab/compose-lab.sh" ownword_compose config --quiet && ownword_compose build app && ownword_compose --profile tools run --rm --no-deps migrate && ownword_compose up -d --no-deps app web && ownword_compose ps Checkpoint. The migration exits successfully and Compose shows app and web running. From the workstation, curl -fsS https://origin-lab.example.com/ -o /dev/null succeeds with a valid origin certificate. If it fails, check the origin A record, Lightsail ports and ownword_compose logs --tail=60 web app.
5. Publish through CloudFront and AWS WAF If you do not have a custom domain, you do not need to rent one for this lab. Skip step 1 (ACM) and step 5 (DNS CNAME), leave Alternate domain names empty in step 2 so CloudFront uses its default *.cloudfront.net certificate, and use https://<distribution>.cloudfront.net for APP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN in deploy/lightsail/.env and for the Cognito callback and sign-out URLs in section 1.
In ACM, N. Virginia, request a public certificate for the public hostname. Add the ACM validation CNAME at your DNS provider and wait for Issued. Keep that CNAME for renewal. Caddy serves the separate origin certificate. CloudFront certificate requirements · ACM DNS validation Create a standard CloudFront distribution for a custom origin. Enter the origin hostname, no origin path, HTTPS only on port 443 for the origin, and Redirect HTTP to HTTPS for viewers. Add your public hostname as an alternate domain name and select the ACM certificate. Select pay-as-you-go for this disposable lab so the distribution can be removed after testing. Origin settings · Distribution settings For the default behavior, allow all HTTP methods so the application can process POST and other writes. Select CachingDisabled and AllViewerExceptHostHeader for the origin request policy. Cookies, query strings and viewer headers pass through, and CloudFront sends the origin hostname in Host so it matches Caddy’s virtual host and certificate. This preserves the OAuth callback, session cookies, and same-origin checks. Use an origin response timeout appropriate to the lab’s AI calls and verify it with real lab requests. Cache behavior settings · Managed cache policies · Managed origin request policies Attach a CloudFront-scope AWS WAF web ACL. For the lab, add a managed rule group such as AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet with its rule actions overridden to Count. After the DNS step, run normal sign-in and Writing requests and review sampled requests before switching to blocking. The web ACL protects traffic served by CloudFront. Associate a WAF web ACL · Test WAF protections When the distribution is Deployed, create a DNS CNAME from the lab’s public subdomain to the distribution hostname, or an alias at Route 53. Keep the origin A record pointed to Lightsail. Run these checks from the workstation with your public hostname. CloudFront alternate domain names LAB_HOST='app-lab.example.com' curl -fsS -D - -o /dev/null "https://$LAB_HOST/" curl -fsS -D - -o /dev/null "https://$LAB_HOST/auth/signin?hosted=1" Checkpoint. The homepage should return 200 through CloudFront. The hosted sign-in URL should send you to Cognito with the public callback. Register and verify a test email through Ownword’s form. Sign in, save a word, and sign out. Then use Google with that verified email for the first time in this pool. You should see the same WordBoard. Try another Google account to make sure it has a separate board. For a 502, check DNS, origin TLS, and the forwarded host. If Cognito rejects the redirect, compare the callback and sign-out URLs character by character.

title: Back up RDS and configure monitoring
content:
1. Give the backup role read access to RDS In the Lightsail SSH session, once the migration in chapter 5.5 finishes, connect using the RDS endpoint and the app owner’s password from chapter 5.4.
cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" RDS_HOST='YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT' docker run --rm -it \ --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-ca.pem,target=/rds-ca.pem,readonly" \ -e PGSSLMODE=verify-full -e PGSSLROOTCERT=/rds-ca.pem \ postgres:16-alpine psql -h "$RDS_HOST" -U ownword_app -d ownword -W Inside psql, first check that the connection uses TLS and that the migration journal has entries. Then give the backup role read access to the app’s tables and sequences, including the Drizzle journal. The default grants also cover objects ownword_app creates later.
\set ON_ERROR_STOP on SELECT current_user, ssl, version FROM pg_stat_ssl WHERE pid = pg_backend_pid(); SELECT count(*) FROM drizzle.__drizzle_migrations; GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE ownword TO ownword_backup; GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public, drizzle TO ownword_backup; GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public, drizzle TO ownword_backup; GRANT SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public, drizzle TO ownword_backup; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public, drizzle GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO ownword_backup; ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public, drizzle GRANT SELECT ON SEQUENCES TO ownword_backup; \q Amazon RDS TLS · PostgreSQL default privileges
2. Create S3 storage and a dedicated backup identity In S3 (Singapore), create a general purpose lab bucket with a unique name. Keep Block all public access and Bucket owner enforced. Enable versioning and SSE-S3. Add a lifecycle rule for daily/ with current expiration after 30 days and noncurrent expiration after 7 days. To reproduce the production access logs, create a second private bucket in the same account and Region, then enable Server access logging on the backup bucket. Use the separate bucket as the destination and verify its policy permits logging.s3.amazonaws.com to write to the selected prefix. Apply a 30-day expiration to the log prefix. Create a bucket · Lifecycle rules · Access logging Create the programmatic IAM identity ownword-lab-backup with a dedicated access key and no console access. Use this inline policy, replacing the bucket name. s3:GetObject covers downloading and checking object metadata. The CloudWatch condition limits metric writes to the workshop’s namespace. HeadObject permissions · CloudWatch IAM conditions { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR_BACKUP_BUCKET/daily/*" }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "cloudwatch:PutMetricData", "Resource": "*", "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"cloudwatch:namespace": "Ownword/Pilot"}} } ] } In the Lightsail SSH session, choose Singapore when aws configure asks for the default Region, and confirm the final identity is the lab backup user.
cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" bash deploy/lightsail/install-aws-cli.sh aws configure --profile ownword-lab-backup chmod 600 "$HOME/.aws/credentials" umask 077 nano deploy/lightsail/.secrets/backup.env nano deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-backup.env chmod 600 deploy/lightsail/.secrets/backup.env deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-backup.env aws sts get-caller-identity --profile ownword-lab-backup Enter these values in deploy/lightsail/.secrets/backup.env:
export AWS_PROFILE=ownword-lab-backup export AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1 S3_BACKUP_BUCKET='YOUR_BACKUP_BUCKET' BACKUP_METRIC_INSTANCE='ownword-lab' If another lab in your account already uses ownword-lab for its metric dimension, choose a different value. Fill in deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-backup.env as shown below.
PGHOST=YOUR_RDS_ENDPOINT PGPORT=5432 PGDATABASE=ownword PGUSER=ownword_backup PGPASSWORD=YOUR_BACKUP_ROLE_PASSWORD When rds-backup.env exists, backup-postgres.sh takes the dump from RDS. It uses the CA at deploy/lightsail/.secrets/rds-ca.pem, the ownword_private Compose network, and the postgres:16-alpine image you pulled in chapter 5.4.
3. Verify the S3 copy and restore it in isolation In the Lightsail SSH session, run the backup and check its freshness. The script checks the archive before uploading it with a SHA-256 checksum, then checks the object size in S3. Look for Verified off-instance backup and BackupFresh=1. S3 upload integrity
cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" bash deploy/lightsail/backup-postgres.sh && bash deploy/lightsail/backup-health.sh Replace the sample filename with the one in your S3 key. The commands download the dump, compare it with the local copy, and restore it into a temporary PostgreSQL container with no external network or published ports. After checking the migration journal and saved words, the script removes the container and the downloaded file. S3 GetObject checksum · PostgreSQL pg_restore
cd "$HOME/ownword-lab" ( set -euo pipefail source deploy/lightsail/.secrets/backup.env umask 077 restore_dir="$(mktemp -d)" restore_container="ownword-lab-restore-$$" started=false cleanup() { if [[ "$started" == true ]]; then docker rm -f "$restore_container" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true fi rm -f -- "$restore_dir/backup.dump" rmdir -- "$restore_dir" } trap cleanup EXIT backup_name='YOUR_BACKUP_FILENAME.dump' aws s3api get-object --region "$AWS_REGION" --bucket "$S3_BACKUP_BUCKET" \ --key "daily/$backup_name" --checksum-mode ENABLED "$restore_dir/backup.dump" >/dev/null cmp -- "deploy/lightsail/backups/$backup_name" "$restore_dir/backup.dump" docker run -d --rm --name "$restore_container" --network none \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" postgres:16-alpine >/dev/null started=true for attempt in {1..30}; do if docker exec "$restore_container" pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres -d postgres >/dev/null; then break fi sleep 1 done docker exec "$restore_container" pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres -d postgres docker exec "$restore_container" createdb -U postgres ownword_restore time docker exec -i "$restore_container" pg_restore --exit-on-error --no-owner --no-acl \ -U postgres -d ownword_restore < "$restore_dir/backup.dump" docker exec "$restore_container" psql -U postgres -d ownword_restore -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \ -c 'SELECT count(*) AS migrations FROM drizzle.__drizzle_migrations' \ -c 'SELECT count(*) AS saved_words FROM public.user_word' ) Confirm that the restore command exits successfully and the queries return counts, then record the elapsed time. After the manual checks pass, use crontab -e under ubuntu to install the jobs below. Confirm the VM uses UTC with timedatectl, and install and enable Ubuntu’s cron package if crontab is missing. The first job runs daily at 23:00 UTC, the second hourly at :15, and the third retries pending manual-word enrichment once a minute.
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin 0 23 * * * /bin/bash "$HOME/ownword-lab/deploy/lightsail/backup-postgres.sh" 15 * * * * /bin/bash "$HOME/ownword-lab/deploy/lightsail/backup-health.sh" * * * * * /usr/bin/flock -n /tmp/ownword-lab-word-enrichment.lock /bin/bash "$HOME/ownword-lab/deploy/lightsail/enrich-manual-words.sh" 4. Configure the encrypted backup alarm In Singapore, create a Standard SNS topic ownword-lab-operator-alerts and confirm an email subscription from your lab inbox. Record its ARN. Reserve the alarm name ownword-lab-backup-stale. Its ARN is arn:aws:cloudwatch:ap-southeast-1:YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:alarm:ownword-lab-backup-stale. Append the following statement to the existing SNS access policy after replacing each placeholder. Keep the topic owner’s existing permissions. CloudWatch to SNS topic policy { "Sid": "AllowOwnwordLabAlarm", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Service": "cloudwatch.amazonaws.com"}, "Action": "sns:Publish", "Resource": "YOUR_TOPIC_ARN", "Condition": { "ArnEquals": {"aws:SourceArn": "YOUR_ALARM_ARN"}, "StringEquals": {"aws:SourceAccount": "YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID"} } } Create a customer-managed symmetric encrypt/decrypt KMS key in Singapore with alias ownword-lab-alerts. Append the following two objects to its existing Statement array, keeping the administrative statements. Enable topic encryption and choose this key. CloudWatch needs those two KMS permissions to publish through the encrypted topic. SNS encryption · KMS permissions for CloudWatch and SNS [ { "Sid": "AllowOwnwordLabAlarmKeyUse", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Service": "cloudwatch.amazonaws.com"}, "Action": ["kms:GenerateDataKey*", "kms:Decrypt"], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "ArnEquals": {"aws:SourceArn": "YOUR_ALARM_ARN"}, "StringEquals": {"aws:SourceAccount": "YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID"} } }, { "Sid": "AllowOwnwordLabTopicKeyUse", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Service": "sns.amazonaws.com"}, "Action": ["kms:GenerateDataKey*", "kms:Decrypt"], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": {"kms:EncryptionContext:aws:sns:topicArn": "YOUR_TOPIC_ARN"} } } ] In CloudWatch, open Alarms and choose Create alarm. Select the custom metric Ownword/Pilot → BackupFresh with the exact Instance dimension from step 2. If it was just emitted, wait for it to show up. Use Minimum, a 1-hour period, Lower than 1, 1 out of 1, and Treat missing data as breaching. Name the alarm as reserved above and choose the encrypted SNS topic for the In alarm action. CloudWatch alarms · Missing metric data 5. Verify alarm delivery In CloudWatch Singapore, BackupFresh is 1 and the Ownword pilot backup alarm is in the OK state.
In Singapore CloudShell, wait until your lab alarm shows OK, then use its exact name to trigger a test. CloudWatch returns to evaluating the metric automatically. Look for a successful action and the email in your inbox. To check the threshold as well, observe what happens when the backup is stale or the metric is missing. SetAlarmState
ALARM='ownword-lab-backup-stale' state="$(aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --region ap-southeast-1 \ --alarm-names "$ALARM" --query 'MetricAlarms[0].StateValue' --output text)" if [[ "$state" == OK ]]; then aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --region ap-southeast-1 \ --alarm-name "$ALARM" --state-value ALARM --state-reason 'Ownword lab email test' else printf 'Wait for the lab alarm to be OK. Current state: %s\n' "$state" fi aws cloudwatch describe-alarm-history --region ap-southeast-1 \ --alarm-name "$ALARM" --history-item-type Action --max-items 5 Check the CloudWatch action history and your inbox for the test alert. If the email doesn’t arrive, look at the error in the history, then check the subscription, SNS policy, and KMS key policy.

title: Self-evaluation
content:
During my First Cloud AI Journey internship, my team and I built Ownword for English learners who recognize words they rarely use. Learners can search for a word by describing an idea, save it to WordBoard, and practice recalling it later. I helped decide how vocabulary and practice should work and helped set up the pilot on AWS.
The Ownword workshop walks through the setup we used, with Lightsail running the app and a private RDS database storing learner data. My work included setting up Google sign-in through Cognito and checking that the backup alert reached the operator. When a lab instruction didn’t match what we saw, my teammates and I checked how the service behaved and worked through the problem together.
My ratings No. Criterion What I assessed Good Fair Average 1 Share of the work How much of the team’s work I took on and completed ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 2 Impact of my work What improved for Ownword or the team because of my work ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 3 Initiative Whether I spotted gaps, suggested changes, or volunteered to help ⬜ ✅ ⬜ 4 Teamwork How well I kept teammates informed, listened, and helped when needed ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 5 Learning efficiency How I used my time when I got stuck and when I asked for help ⬜ ✅ ⬜ 6 Responding to feedback How I used feedback to improve my work ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 7 Understanding AWS basics Whether I can explain what the AWS services I studied do and when to use them ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 8 Applying AWS to Ownword How well the services I helped set up fit the project’s needs ⬜ ✅ ⬜ 9 Meeting deadlines Whether I delivered when promised and flagged delays early ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 10 Prioritizing work Whether I focused on what the team needed most ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 11 Consistency How steadily I made progress and kept my worklog up to date ✅ ⬜ ⬜ 12 Quality of work How well I checked my work and how much rework it left for teammates ⬜ ✅ ⬜ My contribution to Ownword My teammates and I discussed what learners needed from Ownword. I worked out how the vocabulary and practice features should behave, built and revised them, and helped set up and test the AWS pilot.
On the vocabulary side, I noticed that words added by hand had blank definitions on WordBoard and in flashcards, so I asked for the app to save the word right away and fill in the definition in the background. I also proposed showing Vietnamese meanings in the first set of suggestions and making the pronunciation button smaller on WordBoard cards.
For practice and flashcards, I specified keyboard and touch controls for Quick Review and reported a first-letter hint that appeared before the learner asked for it. In sentence practice, learners needed to be free to choose any topic where the word fits, which led to removing the preset topic from the information sent to the grader.
On AWS, I configured Google as a sign-in provider in Amazon Cognito, ran the account-linking deployment in AWS CloudShell, and verified that Google sign-in opened the learner’s existing WordBoard. I also ran the S3 backup setup, applied the KMS fix for the operator alert topic, and confirmed that the test notification reached my inbox after the fix.
Needs improvement I missed several major ways to cut AWS costs. My teammates caught most of them and helped us avoid a more expensive setup, so going forward I need to compare costs earlier while the design is still easy to change. Early in the internship, troubleshooting AWS infrastructure took me too long. Working through problems like missing IAM permissions helped me narrow down causes faster, though I still want to record what I tried more carefully so I do not repeat the same checks. Whenever I learned a new AWS service, I tended to try it on Ownword right away. Some early choices turned out to be a poor fit and had to be replaced once I understood the project and the alternatives better. Next time, I should compare options against what the app needs before adding a service. Even when I tried to keep our Git history tidy and write readable code, some of my changes still caused issues that left my teammates with extra work. Before handing off changes, I need to review them more carefully and explain anything that affects how the team runs or tests the app.

Send a valid request and verify the database Sign in to the lab in the browser. In WordBoard, use the manual add form to save a test word such as lantern. Choose a word the test account has never saved. Reload WordBoard and confirm the word is still there. From the Lightsail SSH session, connect to the lab RDS database with the TLS-protected psql command in chapter 5.6. Run this read-only query with the word you saved. The user_word row shows that the word was saved to a WordBoard. SELECT w.word, uw.stage, uw.added_at FROM public.user_word AS uw JOIN public.word AS w ON w.id = uw.word_id WHERE lower(w.word) = 'lantern' ORDER BY uw.added_at DESC LIMIT 5; Record whether the word is visible after reload and whether RDS returns a row with the expected add time. const invalidWord = await fetch('/api/words/manual', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ word: 42 }), }); console.log(invalidWord.status, await invalidWord.json()); Expect HTTP 400 with a validation message. title: Sharing and feedback
content:
The environment I’d definitely recommend FCAJ to a friend, mainly because of how friendly it felt to learn there. While my team and I were building Ownword, I felt comfortable asking questions and liked being around people who were eager to learn too.
Support from my mentor and the admins Whenever I got stuck or had a question, my mentor and the admins took the time to help. They were patient when I needed something explained again, which made it easier to ask follow-up questions. I appreciated how specific their feedback on Ownword was, because it showed me what to work on next.
Learning through Ownword I enjoyed trying out AWS services with my teammates. One problem I remember was figuring out which IAM permissions were missing. Working through it together helped me see how the services fit together.
The moment I’m proudest of is when we made Ownword available to the public for the first time. We’d spent months building it and working through problems as they came up. It felt good to open the live app and see it finally work the way we’d hoped.
What this means for my career I want to become an AI engineer, and this AWS internship helped me move toward that goal. A lot of AI applications run in the cloud, and building Ownword showed me what it takes to get an app running so other people can use it.
A suggestion A few lab instructions seemed out of date, and sometimes what we saw didn’t match the written steps. We worked through those differences as a team. I’d find the labs easier to follow if those steps were checked and updated more often.
